title: On bended knee for a wooden chapel
original: Conspiciendo nosmet ipsos tam miseram, et non stabilem Capellam habere [...] flexis genibus oramus
translation: Seeing that we have so poor and unsound a chapel [...] we beg on bended knee
why: In January 1803 four villages wrote to their bishop for leave to build a chapel of wood. Their landlord had already given the ground. It is the oldest paper in the archive.
text: In January 1803 four villages wrote to their bishop for leave to build a chapel of wood. Their landlord had already given the ground. It is the oldest paper in the archive.

title: Signed by the scribe
original: Joannes Demko et reliqui incolae Possessionis Viszoka
translation: Joannes Demko and the other inhabitants of the village of Viszoka
why: Every 'signature' on the petition is in one hand. The villagers did not sign; the scribe wrote four names for each village and 'the rest'. The first Demko on paper is one of the four.

title: Explained in Slovak
original: Felolvastatván tót nyelven megmagyaráztatott, helybenhagyatott és aláíratott
translation: Read out, explained in the Slovak language, approved and signed
why: A Hungarian state form of 1906, filled in Hungarian, then explained to the father in Slovak before he signed. He signed his own name.

title: A daughter three days after his birthday
why: If the father is the Mihály baptised in 1882, he was born on 19 August and his daughter on 22 August: he had been 24 for three days when she arrived, and four when he gave his age to the registrar.

title: Mary and Mike
original: IN LOVING MEMORY OF MARY DEMKO BORN 1906 DIED 1950 BELOVED WIFE OF MIKE DUSKA
why: Mária and Mihály left the register books as Mária and Mihály and are cut in stone in Montréal as Mary and Mike. She is named by her maiden surname, under his.

title: Married but once
original: THAT the said Mike Duska was married but once, namely, to the late Dame Maria Demko
why: To sell a property in Québec in 1966 a widower had to declare his whole married life to the notary. That one clause, written sixteen years after she died, is the only paper that gives the day of her death.

title: Two crosses
translation: Mihály and János, each marked with a cross
why: Twins baptised in May 1873, each name followed by a cross. Nine years later the same parents gave the name Mihály again.

title: The younger
why: The priest at Solymos had to write 'the younger' because a father and son of one name lived at Jesztreb. A third Mihály Demkó was growing up at Viszoka and a fourth was a father at Sztrajnyán. All four are within a day's walk.

title: The wrong book
original: Tévedésből vezettetett ide, lásd a [...] könyvébe, a 95. folyó szám alatt.
translation: Entered here by mistake; see the book of [...], under running number 95.
why: A whole baptism written into the wrong register, then left standing with a note saying where it belongs.

title: Georg, struck out
why: A gunner from Galicia died in the epidemic hospital at Košice in March 1915 and was buried the next day. The clerk typed the wrong first name and corrected it by hand. Where the grave is, the card does not know.

title: Samarkand
original: 8. septembra 1915, v táborovej nemocnici v Samarkande
translation: 8 September 1915, in the camp hospital at Samarkand
why: A private from Šariš, buried in Central Asia two days after he died in a camp hospital. The card never says the words 'prisoner of war'.

title: The baptism that became a year
translation: No. 49, then nothing, then '1871' written across the empty cells
why: The priest began a row for a Demko child at the end of 1870, wrote the parents and godparents, and stopped. Then the year turned: he wrote 1871 over the gap, renumbered the next rows from 1, and entered the child three rows down. It looks like a baby with no name. It is a clerk changing his mind.

title: Legitimised a year later
translation: illegitimate [...] legitimised in the month of February 1889
why: Born in February 1888 and entered as illegitimate. Her parents married a year on, and the priest went back to the old page to say so.

title: Seven baptisms, six or seven houses
why: One cottar couple of Jesztreb, Michael Demko and Maria Lazár, brought children to the font seven times from 1864 to 1885 and gave a different house number almost every time. A cottar rented; the family moved with the work.

title: Three churches at one font
original: Kocsis Mihály g.kath. gazda / Knyezső Mária r.kath. [...] Balás Anna ref.
translation: Mihály Kocsis, Greek Catholic farmer; Mária Knyezső, Roman Catholic; [godmother] Anna Balás, Reformed
why: A Greek Catholic father, a Roman Catholic mother and a Reformed godmother, in a village of a few hundred people. The priest noted each one's church beside the name.

title: Without a house
why: The register ranks its fathers: farmer, cottar, and at the bottom the cottar who has not even a house. This one's daughter had a master smith for a godfather.

title: The baptism book kept the deaths too
why: When a small child died, the priest turned back to the baptism entry and wrote the date beside it. Eight of the strips in hand carry such a note, between 1875 and 1894.

title: Two Marys, 1906
translation: Mary Demko (or Danko), 1906 to 199[?], born at Passaic (?), New Jersey
why: If the surname on the chart is Demko: one Mary Demko was born in a village on the Uh in 1906 and died in Montréal, and another was born in New Jersey the same year, came back to the Uh and died there in the 1990s. They crossed the same ocean in opposite directions.

title: György, son of György, godson of György
original: Knyezső György földmíves / Tomócsik Anna [...] Knyezső György / Kontra Anna
translation: [parents] György Knyezső, farmer, and Anna Tomócsik; [godparents] György Knyezső and Anna Kontra
why: Two men called György Knyezső lived at Solymos, told apart only by their wives. In 1890 one couple baptised a son György with the other couple as godparents. In 1894 the other couple baptised their own György and the first wife stood godmother.

title: A second surname to tell the Mihálys apart
why: By 1904 there were so many men called Mihály Knyezső at Solymos that one of them carries a second surname in the register.

title: The parish priest's little son
original: filiolus Adm. Rdi Dni Stephani Demko Parochi Körösfőensis
translation: little son of the Very Reverend Stephanus Demko, parish priest of Körösfő
why: A Demko in holy orders in 1809, bringing his own son to the font, with an advocate and a noblewoman as sponsors. Greek Catholic priests married. The Demkos of Viszoka, six years earlier, were villagers who could not sign a petition.

title: Baptised and confirmed in one go
why: In the Greek church a baby is confirmed at the font, in the same rite. The chaplain at Prešov writes both verbs every time.

title: One priest, two languages
why: In 1909 he signs the Senné register in Hungarian as Barna János, plébános. In 1929, in the same church, he baptises Maria Demko's son and is entered in Slovak as Ján Barna, farár. In between, the village was Szenna, then Ungszenna, then Senné, and the country changed around him.

title: Anna, and Anna again
why: János Kocsis and Anna Halász of Senné named a daughter Anna in 1891 and lost her at two. Fifteen years later they named another daughter Anna and lost her at one. Between the two entries the father goes from farmer to cottar.

title: What she looked like
original: Obličaj: podlhovastá. Barva očí: sivé. Barva vlasov: gaštanové.
translation: Face: oblong. Eyes: grey. Hair: chestnut.
why: Until this passport Maria Demko was a name in registers. A clerk at Michalovce wrote down her face in three words, in Slovak and French, and pinned her photograph over the next page.

title: Marja, with a j
why: She signs across her own photograph, and again below, and again on the contract in Prague. The offices write Maria or Mária; she writes Marja. Her father signed the entry of her birth in 1906.

title: Wholly reliable
original: menovaná sprievodkyňa má výše 24 rokov, je úplne spoľahlivá
translation: the escort named is over 24 years of age and is wholly reliable
why: To take her own eight-year-old son to his father in Canada she needed the consent of a guardianship court. The court's printed form asks only that the escort be over 24 and reliable. She was 31, and the boy's mother.

title: Aged 28
original: your wife, Maria aged 28, and son, Stefan aged 7
why: Ottawa took the ages from her husband's application. The boy's is right; hers is three years short of her passport's. This agent first put that down to a husband long away from home. The owner offers another reading: Mike Duska may have had neither English nor French when he arrived, so the form may have been filled in for him by someone working through an interpreter or a guess (DM-PR-7). Nothing in hand says which.

title: A boy with two birthdays
why: His mother's passport and the court say he was born on 23 October. The parish book, copied out in 1947 and again in 1955, says the 21st, baptised the 26th. The state believed the mother and the church believed the priest.

title: A birthday at St Mary's
why: Her passport says she was born on 22 August 1906. Her husband's family told the census 15 August 1907. From recall, not checked: 15 August is the feast of the Assumption of Mary in the Roman calendar. The house may have remembered only that Maria was born at St Mary's, and guessed the year.

title: Moved in on her wedding day
why: The census asks every person when they came to live in the village. For Maria the answer is the date in the column before it: she left Iňačovce the day she married.

title: What Michael Demko owed
translation: No. 6, Michael Demko: one holding; 52 days of labour with a team or 104 by hand; 2 capons, 2 chickens, 12 eggs
why: The oldest Demko in the file is a line in a table of dues. Read by the printed column heads, from recall: a year of his life owed the convent of Lelesz fifty-two days with his own oxen, two capons, two chickens and a dozen eggs.

title: Two Marias, one birthday
why: At Senné the census was told Maria Dušková was born on 15 August. At Iňačovce, four kilometres off and by another enumerator, it was told that Maria Kočišová was born on 15 August too. Two women called Maria, two houses, one date. It reads less like two birthdays than like a custom: a Maria's day is St Mary's.

title: A stepmother five years older
why: Zuzanna married Michal Demko at seventeen. He was thirty-six, a widower with a daughter of twelve and a son of seven. The daughter was Maria Demko, five years younger than her new stepmother.

title: The mother-in-law who stayed
original: Kočišová Maria / testiná / vdova / rímsko katolícka
translation: Maria Kočišová, mother-in-law, widow, Roman Catholic
why: A Roman Catholic widow of sixty-seven in a Greek Catholic house, entered as the head's mother-in-law, beside a wife young enough to be her granddaughter. Whichever wife was her daughter, she is the oldest person in the file who was still alive when Maria Demko left for Canada.

title: Cholera, ninety years early
original: 73. Aug. 7. János, atyja: Kocsis János zsellér [...] cholera
translation: No. 73. 7 August. János; his father János Kocsis, cottar [...] cholera
why: The file is named 'Death of Janos Kocsis 1783'. The entry is in Hungarian on a numbered form, the boy is the seventy-third burial of the year by early August, and the rows around him say cholera. It is 1873. Two figures changed places in the file name and moved a village epidemic back ninety years, to a time before cholera had been seen in Europe (from recall: it first reached Hungary in 1831).

title: János, János, János
translation: No. 49, 14 December: János, aged 2. / No. 31, 14 June: János, 15 days
why: György Demkó buried a son János, aged two, on 15 December. Twenty-four weeks later his wife bore twins and one was named János. That János was buried on 15 June, his twin Mihály two days before him. In March 1875 the next boy was named János. The name Mihály went the same way: a twin in 1873, an infant of house 121 in a year not yet fixed, and the boy of 1882 who lived (DM-NC-019). The name belonged to the house more than to the child.

title: One sickness, three languages
why: Three women of the Demko houses of Viszoka died of consumption, and the same parish book names it in three languages: Latin for Barbara in [1831], Hungarian for Anna in [1842], the Slavonic of the Greek Catholic church, in Cyrillic, for Maria in 1857. The last is read with some doubt. The book changed its language twice in a lifetime; the sickness in the houses did not change.

title: The priest was not called
original: Demko László kertész, N. Erzsébet férje [...] a lelkész igénybe nem vétetett
translation: László Demko, gardener, husband of Erzsébet N. [...] the priest was not called
why: A gardener of eighty died at Kenyhec. In the column for the last sacraments the priest wrote that nobody had sent for him. He did not know the widow's maiden name either and entered her as 'N.' A man the parish hardly knew, in its own book.

title: The unknown Demko has a name
original: Josephus, parentes Joannes Szmeriga colonus [et] Susana Demko [...] 6.
translation: Josephus; parents Joannes Szmeriga, farmer, and Susana Demko [...] aged 6
why: The file is called 'Death of Unknown Demko 1867'. The boy is named in the first word of the entry: Josephus. He was six and died of smallpox. He is not a Demko either; that is his mother's name. The collector searched for the surname, found it in the row, and kept the row.

title: Nobody in this family knew their birthday
why: Three children of one house were asked their birthdays by the census on one night in 1930, in two villages. The priest had written 29 March, 23 April and 19 August. They said 15 April, 10 April and 28 August. Right year, right month or the next one, wrong day, every time. From recall, not checked: in these villages a person kept the name day, not the birthday. The book in the sacristy was the only thing that knew.

title: Widowed on a date
why: The form has a small line 'b' under the wedding date, for the day a marriage ended. For Barbora it is filled in: 25 March 1915. She had a son of three and another of four months. Fifteen years later she is the owner of the house and the two boys are still with her.

title: Exact match, two thousand years apart
why: Seventeen men are listed as an 'Exact Match' to the owner. It means exact at twelve markers, the cheapest test. The five who paid for the full one differ from him at 25 to 43 places, and the nearest man known on his branch has a paternal line from the plains of northern Poland. The last ancestor they share lived before the Roman Empire.
